facts.claim: "On Tuesdays" is track 10 on the 4onthefloor's debut album 4x4, which runs 2:22. The album came out on Double Asterisk Group on February 8, 2011.
The Bandcamp version of the track is titled "(Drunk) On Tuesdays".
Gabriel Douglas is credited as writer and composer of the live versions of "(Drunk) On Tuesdays", from the 2019 Codfish Hollow and 2021 First Avenue live albums.

4x4 was recorded at Creation Audio (listed on Discogs as Creation Studios) in Minneapolis. Miles Hanson mastered the album. The band called the session quick and said it was the first time all four members had been in a studio together.
Discogs credits the album's recording to Creation Studios.
The 4x4 lineup was Gabe Douglas (vocals, guitar), James Gould (guitar, backing vocals), Chris Holm (bass, harmonica, backing vocals) and Mark Larson (percussion). Each member played a bass drum.
The band writes every song in 4/4 time. Each member plays a kick drum while playing his instrument. This is the idea behind the name and behind the 4x4 title.
In an interview the band rated the difficulty of writing everything in 4/4 at about a 4 out of 10. They said the 4/4 decision was made as the band was forming.
After playing SXSW 2011, the band self-released a double-LP edition of 4x4 in April 2011. Vita.mn named them best new band of 2011.
A&E's Duck Dynasty used the 4x4 track "Workin' Man Zombie" as its theme song.

research.lineage: The 4onthefloor are a Minneapolis band playing stomping, bar-room blues rock with roots-rock and Americana leanings, in a tradition critics compare to the Black Keys, Creedence Clearwater Revival and the North Mississippi Allstars.

draft:
On Bandcamp, the 4onthefloor give this song one more word: **"(Drunk) On Tuesdays."** The streaming title drops the parenthesis, and on its own "On Tuesdays" reads like a standing appointment. Put the word back and it becomes an admission about the least festive night of the week. Nobody gets drunk on a Tuesday for a holiday. That small edit is the emotional key to the track, and the band plays it straight, without a wink and without apology.

Gabe Douglas, who sings and plays guitar in the band, sits in the middle of his range with a raw, unpolished edge. Nothing is smoothed over. In places a second voice slides in underneath with a lower harmony, and it shifts the mood. A weeknight drunk is lonelier sung alone. The harmony sounds like someone on the next stool keeping pace.

Under them the groove moves at a moderate, driving clip. The drums hold a steady beat with a firm backbeat. The bass keeps a simple, repeating line that never reaches for attention. An electric guitar picks a clean arpeggiated figure, then digs into distorted, rhythmic strumming, and the band leans harder as it does. It plays less like a release than a shrug turning into a stomp.

That stomp is the band's whole idea. The 4onthefloor write every song in 4/4, and each of the four members plays a kick drum alongside his own instrument. The name comes from it, and so does the album title, *4x4*. Asked how hard the rule makes songwriting, the band put it at about a four out of ten, which sounds like a joke and a fact at the same time.

*4x4* was their debut, cut quickly at Creation Audio in Minneapolis, the first time all four had been in a studio together. The sound carries that hurry. It is dry, close-miked, gritty and full of energy, with no polish to hide behind.

The tradition here is bar-room blues rock, the line critics draw through Creedence Clearwater Revival, the North Mississippi Allstars and the Black Keys. The song borrows Creedence's economy and is over in under two and a half minutes. It borrows the Keys' close, scuffed recording too. Then it builds all of that on the band's own rule: four players, four kick drums, four beats to the bar.

Douglas is credited as writer on live recordings of the song from Codfish Hollow in 2019 and First Avenue in 2021, so it stayed in the set long after the debut.

It makes an ordinary weeknight feel worth stomping your foot for, without pretending it was ever anything more than an ordinary weeknight.
